summary: Two topics: First, emergency procedures for blood bowl confusion or accidental mixing - if the HP cannot identify which bowl holds bull vs. goat blood, he sprinkles from each bowl in three sequential rounds, ensuring the required service is fulfilled regardless of bowl identity. Blood mixed accidentally into a third bowl is handled similarly. Second, the conclusion of the blood service: the HP pours the remaining blood at the western base of the outer altar, completing the full four-zone Yom Kippur purification circuit.

learning.learnerQuestion: If the High Priest loses track of which bowl holds the bull's blood and which holds the goat's blood during the service, what happens?
learning.coreTension: The bull and goat blood services are distinct with different atonement targets; confusing them would mean applying the wrong blood to each station, potentially invalidating the entire service.
learning.coreMove: The Talmud establishes a coverage protocol for bowl confusion: the HP must complete all required blood acts for all locations using both bowls, systematically covering every station with both bloods to ensure the correct blood is applied even if he cannot identify which bowl is which.

takeaway.text: If bowl confusion occurs during the Yom Kippur blood services, the High Priest follows a systematic coverage protocol: applying blood from each bowl to all stations, ensuring correct coverage even under uncertainty.

learning.learningBlocker: Students may assume bowl confusion simply invalidates the service and requires starting over; the Talmud's solution is a forward-looking systematic coverage approach, not a restart.

learning.ahaMoment: The blood completes its journey from the innermost (kapporet) to the outermost (outer altar base) - a full traversal of Temple sacred space in the service of atonement.
learning.memoryAnchor: Blood's circuit: from the Ark to the outer altar - the entire Temple purified in one Yom Kippur day.
learning.learnerQuestion: After all the sprinkling services are complete, what happens to the remaining blood in the bowls?
learning.coreTension: Blood used in Temple services cannot simply be discarded; there is a specific designated place for disposal, and the manner of disposal (pouring versus sprinkling) is itself a defined act.
learning.coreMove: The Talmud establishes that remaining blood from the Yom Kippur services is poured onto the base (yesod) of the outer altar; this base-pour is a disposal pour, not a sprinkling act, completing the blood service sequence.

takeaway.text: Remaining blood from the Yom Kippur blood services is disposed of by pouring it onto the base (yesod) of the outer altar; this is a designated disposal act, not an additional sprinkling.

learning.learningBlocker: Students may confuse the base-pour with the sprinkling acts and count it as part of the ritual sprinkling sequence; the distinction between a sprinkling act and a disposal pour is important for understanding the total blood-act count.

rashiTranslations.en: 'Cups mixed with cups' - meaning he cannot tell which cup held the bull's blood and which held the goat's.
'He gives, and goes back and gives, and goes back and gives' - for each service he gives one above
and seven below from the first cup, then goes back and gives from the second, then goes back and gives from the first again.
Whichever way you look at it: if the first cup was the bull's and the second the goat's, the obligation is fulfilled by the first and second rounds;
and if the first cup was the goat's, that round is
as though it did not happen, since we learned the bull's blood holds back
the goat's, so the obligation is fulfilled by the second and third rounds, since
the bull must precede the goat, and likewise in the Heichal. 'Some
of the blood got mixed' - meaning some spilled from two
basins into an empty third basin,
while some remained in each of the original two.
'It is obvious to me that when he gives' - he gives the sprinklings with certainty
from what remains in the two original basins. 'However' -
this we must ask: is the blood that mixed in the third basin
treated as leftover, as though it had not mixed, and does it go to the base
of the outer altar, as we learned (Zevachim
47a), that the leftover blood was poured on the
western base of the outer altar? 'Or perhaps'
'it is rejected' - since the initial sprinklings
were not given from it, and it goes instead to the channel in the courtyard
that carries all the courtyard's waste to the
Kidron valley? 'Even according to the one who says' -
in the baraita below, 'one cup, etc.', for example,
he collected the blood in two cups and gave all
the corner-sprinklings from one cup. 'But this one,'
'from which he gives' - since this blood
in the third basin was originally collected in the two basins
from which he gave the sprinklings. 'For it was taught' - this is the dispute
about whether one cup renders its counterpart rejected or leftover,
which we stated above, 'even according to the one who says, etc.'
'Above it says' - regarding the sin offering of
a nasi's goat (Leviticus 4), 'and its blood he shall pour,' etc.,
and regarding the leftover it is written, but the word 'all' is not written here;
whereas below, regarding an individual's sin offering, its own leftover
does have 'all' written. This is the correct reading: from where do we know that for a sin offering whose blood was collected
in four cups, and he gave one sprinkling from this one
and one from that one, that all of them are poured to the base? Scripture states,
'and all of its blood he shall pour.' One might think even if he gave
all four sprinklings from just one of them; Scripture states, 'and
its blood he shall pour' - that one alone is poured to the base, and the others
are poured to the channel. R. Elazar bar R. Shimon says: from where do we know
that for a sin offering whose blood was collected in four cups,
and he gave all four sprinklings from the first cup,
that all of them are poured to the base? Scripture states, 'and all of its blood'
'he shall pour.' The first master holds that one cup renders its counterpart
rejected, while R. Elazar bar R. Shimon holds that one cup
renders its counterpart leftover. 'They are mixed for the corner sprinklings' - the bull's blood is mixed with the goat's blood
when he comes to give the corner sprinklings of the inner altar. 'They are not mixed' -
since he understands 'and he shall take from the blood of the bull and from the blood of the goat' to mean each one separately.
'Who says that even though 'together' is not written, etc.' - for it was taught (Sanhedrin 66a): 'any
man who curses his father or his mother' - I know only of cursing both his father and his mother; from where do I know cursing his father without
his mother, or his mother without his father? Scripture states, 'his father he cursed,' 'his mother he cursed' separately - these are the words of R. Yoshiya.
R. Yonatan says: the verse implies both of them together, and it also implies each one on his own, until
Scripture specifies 'together' elsewhere. This shows that, according to R. Yoshiya, had Scripture not gone on to write 'his father'
'and his mother he cursed' separately, I would have said the opening of the verse implies both together; here too,
'from the blood of the bull and from the blood of the goat' implies both together. 'Since it is written 'once'' -
'and Aaron shall atone upon its horns once a year' (Exodus 30), and not twice. 'It was taught not according to the reversed version' -
but rather as we originally assumed, that it is R. Yoshiya who says they are mixed.
'And he received' - the daf ends here; the comment's own explanation is deferred to 58a, opening the new Mishnah about the receiving-vessel for the blood.
